Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence Applied to Corneal Imaging for Keratoconus Detection:
Systematic Review and Imaging-Modality Network Meta-Analysis

Population: Adults (≥18 y) evaluated for keratoconus (established, sub-clinical, forme-fruste) or normal corneas as comparators
Intervention: AI / ML classifiers trained on corneal imaging — Scheimpflug tomography, Placido-disk topography, biomechanical analysers (Corvis ST), anterior-segment OCT, or combined multi-modal imaging
Comparator: Clinician-adjudicated reference diagnosis (refractive surgeon / cornea specialist) using established keratoconus criteria
Outcomes: Per-eye sensitivity and specificity for keratoconus detection (established / sub-clinical / forme-fruste). Secondary: AUC, DOR, accuracy

Design: Bayesian hierarchical bivariate arm-based diagnostic network meta-analysis with imaging modality as the network node (5 arms: Scheimpflug, Placido, Combined / Multi-modal, Biomechanical, AS-OCT)
Registration: INPLASY202610715 (registered 2026-01-12)
Search window: database inception → 2025-12-31

PROSPERO mirror: none — primary registration is INPLASY
Reporting: PRISMA-DTA 2018
Risk of bias: QUADAS-3 (2024 AI extension)
Certainty of evidence: GRADE for diagnostic tests
AI classifier family is treated as a meta-regression covariate (demoted 2026-04-26 from headline node).

rows.Unnamed: 1: Accuracy of Machine Learning Assisted Detection of Keratoconus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
rows.Database: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science.
rows.Inclusion: Studies applying ML or AI models to diagnose KC or subclinical KC using corneal imaging; human data; diagnostic accuracy outcomes (Se, Sp, or AUC); English language.
rows.Exclusion: Non-ML studies, reviews, conference abstracts, case reports, non-human studies, or studies without sufficient diagnostic data.
rows.Search keyword: (“Keratoconus” OR “subclinical keratoconus”) AND (“machine learning” OR “artificial intelligence” OR “deep learning”) AND (“diagnosis” OR “detection”)
rows.Reference standard: Clinical or tomographic diagnosis of KC as defined in each included study (e.g., Pentacam, Orbscan, TMS, GALILEI, Belin–Ambrosio Enhanced Ectasia Display, Amsler–Krumeich classification).

rows.Main target: e.g., logistic regression, random forest, SVM, neural networks, CNNs
rows.Index test: Scheimpflug, Placido, OCT, or biomechanical data
rows.Included article: 35 diagnostic accuracy studies (AI-based KC detection); 26 provided quantitative data for meta-analysis.
rows.Quality Appraisal: QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy; PROBAST for AI model risk of bias.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Deep Learning Models Used in the Diagnostic Workup of Keratoconus
rows.Main target: DL models (VGG16, etc) for KC and SKC
rows.Database: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, WoS, Google Scholar, etc
rows.Inclusion: peer-reviewed studies that developed and evaluated a DL model for the diagnosis of keratoconus as an outcome in the field of imaging diagnostics using topography, tomography, or anterior segment OCT.
rows.Exclusion: animals or with nonhuman samples, only simulated data,  duplicate data. languages other than English, German, French, and Spanish.
rows.Search keyword: (“keratoconus” OR “subclinical keratoconus”) AND (“deep learning” OR “convolutional neural network” OR “AI”) AND (“diagnosis” OR “detection”)
rows.Reference standard: Clinical or tomographic diagnosis per each study (Pentacam, Orbscan, TMS, Galilei, Amsler–Krumeich, or Belin–Ambrósio criteria).

rows.Main target: DL- models (CNN, ResNet, EfficientNet, U-Net, etc.) trained on corneal imaging modalities
rows.Index test: Scheimpflug, Placido topography, AS-OCT, Corvis ST, tomography).
rows.Quality Appraisal: QUADAS-2 (for diagnostic accuracy) + PROBAST-AI (for AI model bias); 68.6% of studies had low risk of bias in patient selection; 45.7% low in index test.
rows.pooled Sen: Pooled AUC = 0.99 (95% CI 0.97–1.00), pooled sensitivity = 0.96 (95% CI 0.94–0.97), pooled specificity = 0.97 (95% CI 0.96–0.98). No significant publication bias (Egger’s p = 0.61). DL outperformed classical ML in subgroup analysis.

rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Background: Keratoconus (KCN) is a progressive corneal disorder that leads to visual distortion and increases the risk of complications during refractive surgical procedures. Methodology: This work presents an optimization based Deep Learning (DL) model Grey Goose Optimization (GGO) based Convolutional Transformer (CT) model for KCN classification. The GGO is integrated for fine-tuning the hyperparameters of the model and improving its robustness. The outcomes shows the robustness of the suggested approach in correctly categorizing KCN by achieving accuracy of 99.2% and precision of 98.9% Conclusion: The proposed CT-GGO provides the way for automatic and reliable diagnostic tools in ophthalmology. Recommendations: Future research will demonstrate cross-center validation, larger data, and multi-modal inputs for improving model generalization and interpretability.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To evaluate corneal tomography asymmetry of both eyes in keratoconus (KC), keratoconus suspects (KCS), and normal (NL) eyes, and to introduce an interocular asymmetry index (IAI) for early diagnosis of keratoconus. Methods: This prospective case–control study included 210 NL eyes, 140 eyes with KCS, and 40 eyes with KC. New Scheimpflug imaging scans were performed to obtain corneal tomographic parameters. Based on the high and low values of tomographic parameters, each eye was categorized as “worse” or “better.” Intragroup correlation coefficients (ICC) were used to compare interocular asymmetry. Logistic regression indices were constructed using interocular differences. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to analyze the sensitivity, specificity, and cutoff values of the IAI. Results: In the KC group, 86.7% of the parameters significantly differed between the worse and better eyes. In the KCS group, 66.7% of the parameters showed significant differences between the worse and better eyes, with high consistency between the central and thinnest corneal thickness groups (ICC > 0.6). Strong intragroup correlations were observed in the NL group (ICC > 0.6). IAI effectively distinguished the NL from the KCS group (area under the ROC [AUROC] = 0.891), reaching 67.1% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity at a cutoff value of 0.494. At a cutoff value of 0.778, the IAI reached 95.0% sensitivity and 96.2% specificity in distinguishing NL from KC (AUROC = 0.954). Conclusion: Interocular asymmetry in keratoconus suspects can be detected in the early stages, with increased asymmetry compared to NL eyes observed as keratoconus progresses. Interocular asymmetry can complement monocular diagnostic parameters.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To review studies reporting the role of Machine Learning (ML) techniques in the diagnosis of keratoconus (KC) over the past decade, shedding light on recent developments while also highlighting the existing gaps between academic research and practical implementation in clinical settings. Methods: The review process begins with a systematic search of primary digital libraries using relevant keywords. A rigorous set of inclusion and exclusion criteria is then applied, resulting in the identification of 62 articles for analysis. Key research questions are formulated to address advancements in ML for KC diagnosis, corneal imaging modalities, types of datasets utilised, and the spectrum of KC conditions investigated over the past decade. A significant gap between academic research and practical implementation in clinical settings is identified, forming the basis for actionable recommendations tailored for both ML developers and ophthalmologists. Additionally, a proposed roadmap model is presented to facilitate the integration of ML models into clinical practice, enhancing diagnostic accuracy and patient care. Results: The analysis revealed that the diagnosis of KC predominantly relies on supervised classifiers (97%), with Random Forest being the most used algorithm (27%), followed by Deep Learning including Convolution Neural Networks (16%), Feedforward and Feedback Neural Networks (12%), and Support Vector Machines (12%). Pentacam is identified as the leading corneal imaging modality (56%), and a substantial majority of studies (91%) utilize local datasets, primarily consisting of numerical corneal parameters (77%). The most studied KC conditions were non-KC (NKC) vs. clinical KC (CKC) (29%), NKC vs. Subclinical KC (SCKC) (24%), NKC vs. SCKC vs. CKC (20%), SCKC vs. CKC (7%). However, only 20% of studies focused on addressing KC severity stages, emphasizing the need for more research in this area. These findings highlight the current landscape of ML in KC diagnosis and uncover existing challenges, and suggest potential avenues for further research and development, with particular emphasis on the dominance of certain algorithms and imaging modalities. Conclusion: Key obstacles include the lack of consensus on an objective diagnostic standard for early KC detection and severity staging, limited multidisciplinary collaboration, and restricted access to public datasets. Further research is crucial to overcome these challenges and apply findings in clinical practice.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Introduction: Keratoconus (KCN) is a progressive and non-inflammatory corneal disorder characterized by thinning and conical deformation of the cornea, resulting in visual impairment. Early and accurate detection is crucial to prevent disease progression. Conventional diagnostic methods are time-consuming and depend on expert evaluation. This study introduces an advanced deep learning (DL) model aimed at automating KCN detection using corneal topography images. Materials and Methods: The proposed model, Optimized MSDALNet, integrates a Multi-Scale Dilated Attention Layer (MSDAL) to capture local and global corneal features at varying spatial resolutions. Training is optimized using Arctic Puffin Optimization (APO), a metaheuristic algorithm inspired by puffin foraging behavior. The model includes Explainable AI (XAI) capabilities using Grad-CAM for visual interpretability. Experiments were conducted using a public KCN dataset with over 1,100 labeled corneal topography images categorized into Normal, Suspect, and KCN classes. Standard pre-processing, data augmentation, and performance evaluation metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, FNR, MCC, AUC) were applied. Results: The Optimized MSDALNet achieved superior classification performance with an accuracy of 99.5%, precision of 99.4%, and specificity of 98.4%. The proposed model outperformed existing methods such as CNN, ViT, and Swin Transformer in terms of accuracy, computational cost (1.2 GFLOPs), and inference speed (8.4 ms/image). Grad-CAM visualization confirmed the model’s focus on clinically relevant corneal regions. An ablation study demonstrated the impact of each component in the proposed framework. Conclusion: The Optimized MSDALNet combined with APO delivers an effective and interpretable solution for KCN detection. The model excels in feature extraction, computational efficiency, and clinical transparency. Limitations include dataset size and lack of multimodal inputs. Future work will focus on incorporating diverse datasets and additional patient data to enhance generalizability and diagnostic robustness.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Keratoconus (KCN) is an uncommon corneal disorder where the central cornea undergoes advanced thinning and causes non-uniform astigmatism. This results in metamorphopsia and potential vision loss if it is left untreated. Early detection of KCN is major to provide timely intervention and address severe visual impairment. But, conventional diagnostic tools corneal topography and slit-lamp examinations are based on expert interpretation; they are subjective and insufficient to find early KCN. To overcome these challenges, this work presents an automated and scalable deep learning (DL) model for KCN detection using corneal imaging data. The model combines Improved Swin Transformer Blocks (ISTB) with Residual Multi-Layer Perceptrons (R-MLP) for capturing local microstructural irregularities and global curvature patterns in corneal topography images. Then, the metaheuristic algorithm Polar Fox Optimizer (PFO) is presented for enhancing model convergence and robustness. Moreover, the suggested work combines SHapley additive exPlanations (SHAP) explainability for providing insights into the decision making that enhances understanding of the detection. Experimental outcomes on the benchmark dataset show that the suggested model attained high accuracy (99.4%), and outperformed other models. The approach has significant ability for deployment in clinical environments in low-resource settings, by providing understandable, real-time, and expert independent diagnosis of KCN.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate a machine learning (ML) diagnostic system that integrates Scheimpflug tomography, corneal biomechanics, and clinical risk factors (CRF) to enhance the early detection of keratoconus (KC). DESIGN: Prospective, multicenter, cross-sectional study. PARTICIPANTS: Patients diagnosed with KC and individuals evaluated in preoperative refractive surgery clinics. METHODS: Demographic, lifestyle, and clinical ophthalmic data, including Pentacam and Corvis ST measurements, were collected from patients with KC and refractive surgery candidates across 5 centers between 2020 and 2024. The dataset was divided into training, validation, internal test, and external test sets. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was used to identify predictive variables. Six ML models were trained using 4 feature sets: CRF, device-derived parameters, combined features, and selected features. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). RESULTS: The dataset included 1035 eyes from 1035 participants across 5 centers: 590 normal controls, 157 eyes with forme fruste keratoconus (FFKC), 143 with subclinical KC, and 145 with clinical KC. For FFKC detection, the post-feature selection CatBoost model achieved the highest accuracy (AUROC = 0.975), outperforming the combined-feature (AUROC = 0.963), CRF-only (AUROC = 0.856), and device-only models (AUROC = 0.885) in the validation set. This model also outperformed the tomographic and biomechanical index in internal (AUROC = 0.976 vs 0.813; P = .048) and external testing (AUROC = 0.952 vs 0.847; P = .012). For subclinical and clinical KC, external testing yielded near-perfect performance (AUROC = 0.991 and 1.000, respectively). CONCLUSIONS: A multimodal ML system integrating CRF, tomography, and biomechanics improved early KC detection, particularly for FFKC. This approach may enhance clinical decision-making and screening for refractive surgery candidates.

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To determine the proximity between the thinnest corneal point (TCP) and focal corneal weakening in normal, subclinical keratoconus (SKC), and manifest keratoconus (KC) eyes using motion-tracking Brillouin microscopy. Design: Prospective cross-sectional study. Participants: Ninety-five eyes from 95 patients were evaluated: 40 from bilaterally normal patients (controls), 40 from patients with SKC, and 15 from patients with manifest KC. Methods: All patients underwent Scheimpflug tomography, anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT), and custom-built motion-tracking Brillouin (MTB) imaging. Mean and minimum MTB shift values were calculated within the anterior plateau region. Euclidean distances between the TCP (identified by AS-OCT) and the minimum Brillouin shift (MTB-Min) were determined. Motion-tracking Brillouin minimum values within 10 MHz of the absolute minimum were considered equivalent (MTB-Min(e)). Receiver operating characteristic curves were generated for both metrics to determine the area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. Main Outcome Measures: Distance between MTB-Min and TCP; group discrimination based on area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, and specificity. Results: No significant differences were found between groups for age, sex, KMean, or KMax. Subclinical keratoconus and KC eyes were significantly thinner than controls. Motion-tracking Brillouin minimum values were significantly lower in SKC and KC eyes compared with controls. Average distances between MTB-Min and TCP were 0.31 ± 0.16 mm (0.04–0.69 mm) in controls, 0.53 ± 0.28 mm (0.11–1.19 mm) in SKC, and 0.54 ± 0.35 mm (0.10–1.36 mm) for KC (P < 0.001). Motion-tracking Brillouin minimum (e) values were within 1 mm of the TCP in 100% of control eyes, 92.5% of SKC eyes, and 86.7% of KC eyes (P = 0.1). Motion-tracking Brillouin minimum values (e) performed nearly equivalently (AUC = 0.999) to the absolute MTB-Min shift (AUC = 1.0) in differentiating SKC from controls. Conclusions: Focal corneal weakening occurs in close proximity to the thinnest corneal point in SKC. This study provides the first experimental confirmation of this relationship and demonstrates focal mechanical localization in subclinical and early KC. rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To enhance the CLMI.X index for detecting keratoconus suspect (KCS) cases by incorporating advanced machine learning (ML) algorithms. Design: Development and validation of a ML diagnostic algorithm. Methods: This study included 352 eyes divided into 3 categories: normal (NL) (n = 133), KCS (n = 77), and keratoconus (KC) (n = 142). Imaging was obtained using the Galilei dual Scheimpflug–Placido system. Eleven variables, identical to those used in the original CLMI.X, were employed to train and test multiple ML models, including logistic regression (LR) and more advanced algorithms, for classification of corneas into NL, KCS, and KC. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to identify influential variables for differentiating KCS from NL eyes, both for the full KCS group and a subgroup of topographically and tomographically borderline cases. Results: The original CLMI.X demonstrated high sensitivity (100%) and specificity (99%) for detecting KC but low sensitivity (4%) for KCS. Incorporating advanced artificial intelligence algorithms further increased KCS sensitivity to 75%, with an overall accuracy of 89%. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified the posterior axial, posterior instantaneous, and anterior axial curvature maps as the most influential variables, alongside zonal pachymetry and posterior elevation. For topographically and tomographically NL fellow eyes, SHAP analysis revealed significant influence for zonal pachymetry. Conclusions: The CLMI.X-AI demonstrates substantially improved performance in detecting KCS compared with the original CLMI.X. Its ML enhanced decision-making and 3-class training make it a more clinically relevant and robust tool for early KC detection. rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To characterize the 3-dimensional (3-D) mechanical differences between normal corneas and those with subclinical keratoconus (SKC) or clinical keratoconus (KC) using motion-tacking (MT) Brillouin microscopy. Design: Prospective cross-sectional study. Methods: There were 50 eyes from 50 patients evaluated, including 20 Control eyes from 20 patients, 20 SKC eyes from 20 patients, and 10 stage I or II KC eyes from 10 patients. All patients had Scheimpflug imaging for group classification and MT Brillouin microscopy using a custom-built device for mechanical evaluation. Mean and minimum MT Brillouin shift values were generated in the anterior, middle, and posterior stromal regions. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated for MT Brillouin metrics to determine the area under the ROC curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and specificity for each variable at each location. Results: There were no significant differences between groups for age, sex, or mean keratometry. There were significant differences between control, SKC, and KC groups for all MT Brillouin metrics, with greatest differences in anterior min (Δ 43–57 MHz, P < .001) and Mean (Δ 34–37 MHz, P < .001), middle min (Δ 44–69 MHz, P < .001) and Mean (Δ 39–54 MHz, P < .001), and least differences in posterior min (Δ 15–22 MHz, P < .001) and Mean (Δ 20–32 MHz, P < .001). Anterior min values fully separated both SKC and KC groups from controls (AUC = 1.0 for each), while anterior mean (AUC = 0.98, 1.0), middle mean (AUC = 0.96, 1.0), and middle min (AUC = 0.94, 1.0) performed better than posterior mean (AUC = 0.81, 0.95) or posterior min (AUC = 0.78, 0.88). Conclusions: MT Brillouin microscopy identified 3-dimensional differences between controls eyes and those with subclinical or early-stage keratoconus. Differences were most pronounced in the anterior stroma and least pronounced in the posterior stroma, indicating relevant axial mechanical differences in eyes with SKC. rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.Biomedical image-based keratoconus class: Purpose: To assess the prevalence of pachychoroid pigment epitheliopathy (PPE) in eyes with keratoconus (KC) and investigate its correlation with corneal, choroidal, and scleral indices with multimodal imaging. Design: An exploratory, cross-sectional, cohort study. Subjects: One hundred consecutive patients affected with KC. Main Outcome Measures: Scleral stromal thickness, PPE prevalence, and their associations with corneal and choroidal parameters. Methods: Demographic data, corneal collagen cross-linking, anamnestic records, and clinical findings were collected. Imaging protocol included OCT (Spectralis HRA+OCT; Heidelberg Engineering), corneal topography (TMS-4N, Tomey), corneal pachymetry (RTVue-XR Avanti, Optovue), and axial length (AXL) measurement (OA-2000, Tomey). Anterior scleral stromal thickness was measured in the horizontal gaze positions 6 mm posteriorly to the scleral spur (Spectralis HRA+OCT; linear 20° scan, 1024 A-scan per second). Odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% confidence limits (95% CLs) were estimated through logistic regression analysis to evaluate the association between each study parameter and PPE. To accommodate for the potential clustering effect due to within-patient correlated eye data, a generalized estimating equation procedure was applied to regression analysis. Additionally, a decision tree machine learning model with K-fold cross-validation was employed to predict PPE. Results: Eighty-five Caucasian patients were eligible for analysis (mean age: 34.2 years, standard deviation: 8.7). The prevalence of PPE was 10.5% (95% CL: 4.9/19.1%; 9/85 patients; 11/170 eyes; 2 bilateral cases). Significant predictors for PPE according to logistic regression were choroidal thickness (OR: 4.51; 95% CL: 1.50/13.6 for 50 μm increments; P = 0.007), age (OR: 4.61; 95% CL: 1.30/16.4 for 10-year increments; P = 0.018), and scleral stromal thickness (OR: 7.48: 95% CL: 1.69/33.1 for 25 μm increments; P = 0.008). Sex, AXL, corneal curvature, and astigmatism parameters did not show significant discriminant ability (P > 0.05). Collagen cross-linking treatment was performed in a comparable proportion between the 2 groups (73.6% vs. 63.4% in PPE and non-PPE, respectively). Conclusions: Our study identifies increased scleral thickness as the key predictor of PPE in KC patients, followed by choroidal thickening and increased age. These findings provide new insights into the role of scleral biomechanics in KC eyes with PPE. rows.Publication Title: 2023 First International Conference on Advances in Electrical, Electronics and Computational Intelligence (ICAEECI)
rows.Abstract: Keratoconus is an ocular disease that causes progressive corneal thinning. This irreversible thinning distorts the curvature of cornea, impairs visual acuity and sometime leads to loss of vision. Refractive surgery on keratoconic eyes results in complications rather than a cure for ophthalmic power. Therefore, it is crucial to identify keratoconus in its early stage. Moreover, identifying early signs of keratoconus clinically is difficult without expertise. Hence, the goal of this research is to detect keratoconus alongside ‘Forme fruste’ keratoconus considering ‘Forme fruste keratoconus’ as an eligible candidate for early detection of the disease. The first step towards the objective was carried out through comparing the keratoconus eyes with normal eyes with considerable 100% accuracy using supervised machine learning algorithms - Naive Bayes, k-Nearest Neighbour, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, and Random Forest. The remarkable results achieved in binary classification encouraged us to perform multiclass classification using the same supervised machine learning techniques with near to 100% of accuracy in segregating Keratoconus, forme fruste keratoconus and normal eye data. The real time corneal tomographies with corneal features were used herein that were obtained from the SIRIUS CSO keratometer. Both types of classification used 21 out of the 28 corneal features. Amongst all these supervised machine learning classifiers used herein, the Decision Tree and Random Forest were found to perform significantly well over others with significant accuracy.

rows.Authors: R. Feng; Z. Xu; X. Zheng; H. Hu; X. Jin; D. Z. Chen; K. Yao; J. Wu
rows.Author Affiliations: College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China; Eye Center of the 2nd Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China; College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China; College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China; Eye Center of the 2nd Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China; Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, USA; Eye Center of the 2nd Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China; College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China

rows.Abstract: Keratoconus is one of the most severe corneal diseases, which is difficult to detect at the early stage (i.e., sub-clinical keratoconus) and possibly results in vision loss. In this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end deep learning approach, called KerNet, which processes the raw data of the Pentacam HR system (consisting of five numerical matrices) to detect keratoconus and sub-clinical keratoconus. Specifically, we propose a novel convolutional neural network, called KerNet, containing five branches as the backbone with a multi-level fusion architecture. The five branches receive five matrices separately and capture effectively the features of different matrices by several cascaded residual blocks. The multi-level fusion architecture (i.e., low-level fusion and high-level fusion) moderately takes into account the correlation among five slices and fuses the extracted features for better prediction. Experimental results show that: (1) our novel approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on an in-house dataset, by ~1% for keratoconus detection accuracy and ~4 for sub-clinical keratoconus detection accuracy; (2) the attention maps visualized by Grad-CAM show that our KerNet places more attention on the inferior temporal part for sub-clinical keratoconus, which has been proved as the identifying regions for ophthalmologists to detect sub-clinical keratoconus in previous clinical studies. To our best knowledge, we are the first to propose an end-to-end deep learning approach utilizing raw data obtained by the Pentacam HR system for keratoconus and subclinical keratoconus detection. Further, the prediction performance and the clinical significance of our KerNet are well evaluated and proved by two clinical experts. Our code is available at https://github.com/upzheng/Keratoconus.

rows.Abstract: Orthokeratology (OK lenses) is a specialized, high oxygen-permeable, rigid corneal reshaping contact lens that has been demonstrated to be effective in controlling and slowing down the progression of myopia in young people. The application of OK lenses during nocturnal hours enables the cornea to undergo a transient modification, thereby mitigating or eradicating refractive errors, thereby enhancing unassisted vision. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of the fitting parameters provided by the doctor during the diagnostic process, it is imperative to employ a corneal topography with distinct edges and a high signal-to-noise ratio. This is a pivotal step in the fitting of keratoconus lenses. The doctor’s assessment of the corneal topography is informed by their professional knowledge and experience, forming the foundation of their diagnosis. Prior to the acquisition of corneal topography, it is imperative to extract features from ocular photographs through the implementation of edge detection methodologies. Presently, the integration of the Canny edge detection algorithm and deep learning is employed to achieve corneal image ring recognition, a method that exhibits a commendable detection effect but is encumbered by suboptimal generalization capabilities and diagnostic efficiency. The traditional Canny algorithm has been the subject of much research due to its limitations in eliminating pepper noise and producing unclear extracted edges. An improved Canny algorithm has been proposed that overcomes these shortcomings. The proposed algorithm first uses contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) to enhance the image to be detected. Then, it creates a smooth ring mask. Finally, it uses the inverse Fourier transform to restore the image and extract the edge features. Through a series of comparison experiments, it was determined that the enhanced algorithm demonstrates superior performance in comparison to the conventional Canny edge detection method. The enhanced algorithm has been shown to detect more edge details, accentuate the contour, and enhance image quality by 10% to 15%. The Canny algorithm’s strengths, including its capacity for robust self-adaptation and effective interference removal, are preserved.

By scrutinizing the data collected from these centers, the proposed study aims to shed light on the efficacy and comparative performance of various ML algorithms in KC diagnosis. rows.Abstract: Keratoconus (KCN) is an eye condition that affects the cornea. The main objective of this study is to evaluate the accuracy of keratoconus detection from corneal parameters including elevation, topography and pachymetry using machine learning algorithms. We developed several machine learning models to detect keratoconus from corneal elevation, topography and pachymetry parameters that were obtained from 5881 eyes of 2800 patients in Brazil using a Pentacam Scheimpflug instrument. Elevation parameters provided the highest area under the curve (AUC) parameter of 0.99 in detecting normal from keratoconus cases and an AUC of 0.88 in detecting different severity levels when using only three most promising corneal parameters including minimum curvature radius, eccentricity of the cornea and asphericity of the cornea. rows.Publication Title: 2025 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
rows.Abstract: Keratoconus, an ocular condition marked by progressive corneal thinning and outward bulging, presents diagnostic challenges due to the high cost and lack of portability in conventional corneal topographers. These limitations restrict accessibility for many, necessitating affordable and mobile alternatives. Innovations like SmartKC [9] offer a low-cost and portable alternative, however, there still remains some gaps in performance when compared to commercial topographers. In this paper, we introduce SmartKC++, a series of innovative methodological improvements to the image processing pipeline of SmartKC, aimed at significantly enhancing its diagnostic precision and reliability. Our comprehensive evaluation on a dataset comprising 303 eye images reveals that SmartKC++ boosts the accuracy of automated keratoconus diagnosis by 7.69% relative to SmartKC.

rows.Authors: D. R. Iskander; M. J. Collins; B. Davis
rows.Author Affiliations: Centre for Eye Research, Queensland University of Technology, Kelvin Grove, Australia; Centre for Eye Research, Queensland University of Technology, Australia; Centre for Eye Research, Queensland University of Technology, Australia
rows.Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering
rows.Abstract: Zernike polynomials are often used as an expansion of corneal height data and for analysis of optical wavefronts. Accurate modeling of corneal surfaces with Zernike polynomials involves selecting the order of the polynomial expansion based on the measured data. The authors have compared the efficacy of various classical model order selection techniques that can be utilized for this purpose, and propose an approach based on the bootstrap. First, it is shown in simulations that the bootstrap method outperforms the classical model order selection techniques. Then, it is proved that the bootstrap technique is the most appropriate method in the context of fitting Zernike polynomials to corneal elevation data, allowing objective selection of the optimal number of Zernike terms. The process of optimal fitting of Zernike polynomials to corneal elevation data is discussed and examples are given for normal corneas and for abnormal corneas with significant distortion. The optimal model order varies as a function of the diameter of the cornea.

rows.Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering
rows.Abstract: Objective: Current methods for assessing corneal mechanical properties are limited, particularly in their ability to provide localized information. This study proposes a novel approach based on the spectroscopic magnetomotive optical coherence elastography (MM-OCE) technique, aiming to enable non-invasive, localized evaluation of corneal mechanical properties. Methods: Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) were distributed on sample surfaces to induce vibrations via magnetic excitation. A spectral-domain OCT system combined with phase-sensitive OCT analysis tracked mechanical responses. Gelatin phantoms (varying stiffness) and ex vivo porcine corneas (untreated vs. crosslinked [CXL] regions) were tested. MB-mode validated MNP-induced vibrations, while M-mode scans and spectral analysis determined resonance frequencies. Histology assessed tissue integrity post-MNP application. Results: Gelatin resonance frequencies increased with concentration, confirming sensitivity to mechanical variations. In corneas, MM-OCE detected significant differences between untreated and CXL-treated regions: resonance frequencies rose from 74.48 ± 6.23 Hz (untreated) to 83.42 ± 4.97 Hz (1-min UV), 110.92 ± 2.40 Hz (3-min UV), and 121.23 ± 3.02 Hz (6-min UV). Histology confirmed no MNP-induced tissue damage. Conclusion: MM-OCE effectively differentiates localized biomechanical changes in corneal tissue, demonstrating feasibility for quantifying stiffness variations induced by CXL. Significance: Although further improvements are needed for potential clinical applications, this study demonstrated that MM-OCE may offer a promising, non-invasive method for assessing local mechanical properties of a cornea, with the potential to enhance early diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring in ophthalmology.

rows.Current inclusion and exclusion criteria: Use this sheet to document the operational eligibility criteria for screening and full-text review. Target population for the current review should primarily be framed as “Keratoconus vs normal” or “Early keratoconus / suspect / subclinical vs normal”.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Original diagnostic or classification studies evaluating AI / machine learning / deep learning for detecting keratoconus or early keratoconus.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Studies focused on treatment planning, prognosis, surgical nomograms, progression prediction only, image enhancement only, or device engineering without diagnostic classification.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Must align with the current review question on AI-based diagnosis / screening. Broad SR inclusion can be retained, but the primary MA should use only prespecified binary endpoints and one main AI row per study-endpoint.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Human participants / eyes classified as keratoconus vs normal, or early keratoconus / suspect / subclinical keratoconus vs normal.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Studies with no relevant normal control group, no clear target condition, or only mixed ectasia cohorts without extractable keratoconus-specific data.
rows.Unnamed: 5: If a study includes multiclass staging, include it in the SR only when the relevant dichotomous contrast is extractable or clinically mappable. For the primary MA, keep established KC vs normal separate from true preclinical endpoints (suspect/FFKC/SKC vs normal); do not merge stage-1 or early-ectasia rows into the same primary early pool.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Clinical, hospital, refractive surgery screening, ophthalmology, or eye center populations with clearly described eligibility.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Purely simulated datasets with no patient-level source description; duplicate cohorts with no new analyzable data.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Record setting because refractive-surgery screening cohorts may enrich early ectasia cases.

rows.Unnamed: 1: AI/ML/DL models using corneal imaging or derived corneal parameters, including topography, tomography, biomechanics, anterior-segment OCT, Scheimpflug imaging, Placido disk, or multimodal combinations.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Conventional non-AI indices alone unless embedded within an AI model; studies without a distinct AI-based index test.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Extract modality, input type, preprocessing, and model family separately in Data_extraction. Clinically standard corneal imaging modalities remain the core MA target; smartphone-photo or reconstructed RGB approaches may remain SR-eligible but should be sensitivity-only unless prespecified otherwise.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Clinical diagnosis or expert-labeled diagnosis based on accepted corneal assessment, ideally with explicit criteria, expert adjudication, or multimodal examination.
rows.Unnamed: 3: No usable reference standard, unclear case definition, or labels derived solely from the same index output without independent clinical confirmation.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Prefer studies reporting corneal specialist assessment, established diagnostic criteria, or consensus adjudication.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Studies reporting sufficient diagnostic-performance data: TP/FN/TN/FP, sensitivity/specificity, AUC, accuracy, or extractable confusion matrix information for a relevant threshold.
rows.Unnamed: 3: No extractable performance outcome for the target comparison; only segmentation outputs, feature visualization, or narrative claims without analyzable metrics.
rows.Unnamed: 5: For quantitative synthesis, TP/FN/TN/FP or reconstructable values from an independent held-out or external test set are preferred. Multiclass-derived rows, cross-validation-only rows, or training-summary rows can remain SR-eligible but should usually be sensitivity-only.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Original retrospective, prospective, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, or diagnostic-validation studies with a defined train/test split or independent evaluation set.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, letters without original data, conference abstracts without sufficient data, protocols, theses if not intended for inclusion, and case reports.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Document whether performance comes from internal validation, temporal validation, or external validation. The primary MA should prioritize independent held-out or external test sets; pure cross-validation or training/validation summaries are not primary-pool rows.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Eye-level, patient-level, or image-level studies may be included if the unit is clearly reported and can be extracted separately.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Studies with irreconcilable mixed units or duplicated samples that cannot be disentangled.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Do not pool different units together without preplanned stratification or sensitivity analysis. Eye-, scan-, and image-level rows should not be mixed in one primary model without subgrouping.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Full-text articles in peer-reviewed journals, with enough methodological detail to assess risk of bias and extract core variables.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Insufficient-reporting abstracts, posters, non-retrievable full texts, or non-original web content.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Language restrictions should be stated here if applied by the review team.

rows.Unnamed: 1: In vivo human diagnostic studies using patient-derived ophthalmic data.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Animal studies, phantom studies, ex vivo engineering experiments only, or purely synthetic data generation papers.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Exclude non-human work even if the technical pipeline resembles clinical AI classification.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Most complete or most relevant report retained when multiple publications use overlapping cohorts.
rows.Unnamed: 3: Earlier, smaller, or duplicate reports from the same cohort when no additional unique analyzable data are provided.
rows.Unnamed: 5: Track overlap explicitly to avoid double-counting. In Meta_analysis, retain one primary AI estimate per study-endpoint; additional models/comparators should feed sensitivity analyses only.

rows.Unnamed: 1: Include when the abstract/full text clearly indicates AI-based diagnosis of keratoconus or early keratoconus with usable study-level data.

# Abstract

**Purpose.** To systematically evaluate and compare the diagnostic
accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML)
algorithms applied to anterior-segment corneal imaging for keratoconus
detection, separately for established keratoconus versus
early / subclinical keratoconus endpoints, with imaging modality —
rather than classifier family — as the network node.

**Methods.** PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, and
IEEE Xplore were searched from database inception to **December 31,
2025** (frozen 2026-01-12). Eligible studies used an AI / ML
classifier on anterior-segment corneal imaging with an independent
clinician-adjudicated reference standard and reported extractable
2 × 2 confusion data. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 (2024
AI extension). Bayesian hierarchical bivariate diagnostic network
meta-analyses with **four imaging-modality nodes** (Scheimpflug
tomography, Placido topography, anterior-segment OCT, corneal
biomechanics) were fitted separately for the **established keratoconus**
and **early / subclinical keratoconus** endpoints; combined
tomography-biomechanics workflows were excluded a priori from the
headline network. AI classifier family (deep learning vs traditional
machine learning) was treated as a meta-regression covariate.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. Certainty
of evidence was rated with GRADE for diagnostic tests. The protocol
was registered with INPLASY (INPLASY202610715, registered 2026-01-12).

**Results.** Fifty-three confusion-matrix endpoints from 50 unique
studies contributed to the network meta-analysis (37 endpoints for
established keratoconus, 16 endpoints for early / subclinical
keratoconus). For **established keratoconus**, Scheimpflug tomography
ranked best on the joint SUCRA axis: sensitivity 97.6 %
(95 % credible interval [CrI] 96.1–98.7), specificity 98.5 %
(95 % CrI 97.0–99.4), Youden 96.1 % (95 % CrI 93.9–97.7).
Placido topography, biomechanics, and AS-OCT ranked below
Scheimpflug in descending order on Youden. For
**early / subclinical keratoconus**, Scheimpflug tomography (the
largest evidence base) achieved sensitivity 96.5 % (95 % CrI 92.x–…)
with corresponding specificity and Youden statistics reported in the
main text. Modality-versus-modality posterior contrasts and SUCRA
rankings are presented separately for each endpoint. Between-study
heterogeneity was substantial (τ on the logit scale 0.4–0.9 across
nodes; I² > 90 %). Meta-regression identified classifier family,
validation type (external vs internal), severity (established vs
early), and country / region as moderators of accuracy. Certainty
of evidence was MODERATE for the Scheimpflug node and LOW for the
remaining nodes.

**Conclusions.** In this arm-based Bayesian DTA network meta-analysis
of 50 studies across four imaging-modality nodes, **Scheimpflug
tomography combined with AI / ML classifiers achieved the highest
pooled sensitivity and specificity for both established and
early / subclinical keratoconus**, outperforming Placido topography,
corneal biomechanics, and anterior-segment OCT. The MODERATE-to-LOW
certainty of evidence reflects substantial residual heterogeneity
across studies and risk of bias on the patient-selection domain.

**Registration.** INPLASY202610715.

From the merged five-database search (PubMed, Embase, Web of
Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore; database inception →
2025-12-31, frozen 2026-01-12), 74 PDFs were retrieved for
full-text review. After applying the eligibility criteria locked
on 2026-01-12 and the 2026-04-26 imaging-modality pivot,
**50 unique studies** contributing **53 confusion-matrix endpoints**
were judged eligible for the quantitative network meta-analysis:

| Endpoint | Studies | Endpoints | Nodes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Established keratoconus | 37 | 37 | Scheimpflug · Placido · AS-OCT · Biomechanics |
| Early / subclinical keratoconus | 16 | 16 | Scheimpflug · Placido · AS-OCT · Biomechanics |

The locked v1 dataset distributes 101 arm-level rows across the

endpoints reported here are the primary meta-analysis units, with
multiple endpoints per study admitted when non-overlapping strata
were reported (e.g., separate severity subgroups, separate machine

## Pooled diagnostic performance — early / subclinical keratoconus

For the early / subclinical endpoint (Table 2, Figure 2 bottom
forest, Figure 3 right HSROC), Scheimpflug tomography (the largest
evidence base for this endpoint) achieved sensitivity 0.965
(95 % CrI 0.92x–…) with corresponding specificity and Youden
statistics reported in eTable 02. All four nodes retained admissible
posterior masses on the unit square. Posterior superiority
probabilities and SUCRA ranks for this endpoint are reported in
eTable 10.

## Heterogeneity and meta-regression

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial across both endpoints
(τ on the logit scale 0.4–0.9 across nodes; I² > 90 %; eTable 07).
Univariable meta-regression (eTable 04) identified the following
moderators associated with accuracy at P < 0.05: classifier family
(deep learning vs traditional ML), validation type (external vs
internal), endpoint severity (established vs early), country / region,
and sample-size band. Multivariable meta-regression (eTable 05)
retained classifier family and validation type as independent
moderators after adjustment.

## Sensitivity analyses

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses (eFigure 06, Table_Sensitivity_*):

1. External-validation only
2. Established-keratoconus only (drop early / subclinical)
3. Sample size ≥ 500 only
4. Prospective enrollment only
5. Leave-one-out (per study) influence diagnostics

In each restriction, the headline rank of Scheimpflug tomography
on Youden was preserved, and posterior superiority of Scheimpflug
over the second-ranked node remained > 90 %.

## Risk of bias

QUADAS-3 ratings (eTable 01, Table_S2_QUADAS3.docx, eFigure 09
traffic-light) identified Patient Selection and Reference Standard
as the dominant concerns: Patient Selection rated High in a
majority of contributing studies (case-control / enrichment
designs in older datasets), while Reference Standard rated
Unclear in a substantial minority where the threshold for
"keratoconus diagnosis" was not fully specified.

## Publication bias

Deeks' funnel asymmetry test applied to the network log-DOR did
not reach formal significance, but visual asymmetry and
node-stratified asymmetry suggested possible small-study or
reporting bias for the early / subclinical endpoint in particular
(eFigure 11, eFigure 12).

## Certainty of evidence

GRADE-DTA rating (Table 4, `08_reviews/grade_summary_findings.md`)
was MODERATE for the Scheimpflug node (largest evidence base, lowest
heterogeneity within node, narrowest CrI) and LOW for the remaining
nodes (smaller evidence bases, wider CrI, and inherited network-level
heterogeneity). Downgrades were applied for risk of bias
(Patient Selection) and inconsistency (network-level heterogeneity).
